newsitem.title: USA: Armey says Gingrich will win re-election as Speaker.
newsitem.headline: Armey says Gingrich will win re-election as Speaker.

text.p: House Majority Leader Dick Armey on Sunday predicted Newt Gingrich will be easily re-elected speaker despite his violation of House rules in giving inaccurate information to an ethics investigation.
Armey told NBC's "Meet the Press" it would vote on a penalty against the Georgia Republican prior to the Jan. 7 election for speaker.
Armey said he had "not one bit of doubt" Gingrich would win re-election and promised a unanimous vote by fellow Republicans.
"He will definitely be re-elected," Armey told NBC's "Meet the Press" programme.

Gingrich on Saturday admitted "with great sadness" that he provided inaccurate information to the ethics committee. He also accepted responsibility for failing to seek advice on whether a college course he taught complied with laws barring use of tax-exempt foundations for partisan purposes.
The developments came less than three weeks before Gingrich goes before the full House as a candidate to be the first Republican speaker to be re-elected in 68 years.
The findings -- the result of a two-year investigation by a four-member panel of the bipartisan ethics committee -- were certain to cast a shadow over the Jan. 7 election.

But House Republicans have rapidly closed ranks behind Gingrich, pledging their "unequivocal support" for his re-election. Key Democrats, including House Whip David Bonior, Gingrich's chief critic, say Gingrich should step down.
Former New York governor Mario Cuomo, also appearing on "Meet the Press," said Gingrich had accepted responsibility and needed to "pay the price."
"Put your actions where your words are -- step down," Cuomo said.
Representative John Conyers, ranking Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee, said the Justice Department should get involved since there were "serious legal questions at stake."
President Clinton has declined comment on the matter.

The full 10-member committee must decide whether to recommend to the full House any penalty for infractions of House rules. Punishments can range from a reprimand to a more severe "censure," all the way up to expulsion from the House.

The charges centred on the activities of GOPAC, a political action committee formerly headed by Gingrich, his college course called "Renewing American Civilisation" and the role played by tax-exempt nonprofit foundations.

Armey counselled against trying to second-guess the outcome of the committee's vote, but said a vote to censure Gingrich, which would require him to step down as speaker, would be incomensurate with the errors he admitted.

"I think it will be resolved, certainly before the 7th of January," Armey said. "I do not believe that censure would be appropriate for the errors that were made that the speaker has readily accepted responsibility for."
He was anxious to see the matter resolved: "We need to get this behind us and get on with the serious work before us ... about balancing the budget, improving education and so forth."
